questions.prompt: Which set gives the fermionic Matsubara frequencies $\omega_n$ at inverse temperature $\beta$?
questions.solution: Fermionic functions are antiperiodic in $\tau$, so $e^{i\omega_n\beta}=-1$, which requires odd multiples of $\pi/\beta$ (Eq. 11.28). The set $2n\pi/\beta$ is the bosonic one. The last option has the wrong dimension.

questions.prompt: For fermions and bosons alike, the Matsubara function obeys $\mathcal C_{AB}(\tau-\beta)=\pm\mathcal C_{AB}(\tau)$ for $0<\tau<\beta$. Show this and state the sign for each statistics.
questions.solution:
Write $\mathcal C_{AB}(\tau)=-\langle T_\tau A(\tau)B\rangle$ with $\langle X\rangle=\mathrm{Tr}[e^{-\beta H}X]/Z$. Let $\varepsilon=+1$ for bosons and $\varepsilon=-1$ for fermions.

For $\tau-\beta<0$ the time ordering puts $B$ first, so $T_\tau[A(\tau-\beta)B]=\varepsilon\,B\,A(\tau-\beta)$ and
$$\mathcal C_{AB}(\tau-\beta)=-\varepsilon\,\langle B\,A(\tau-\beta)\rangle .$$
Cyclicity of the trace gives $\mathrm{Tr}[e^{-\beta H}B\,A(\tau-\beta)]=\mathrm{Tr}[A(\tau-\beta)\,e^{-\beta H}B]$. Since $e^{\beta H}A(\tau-\beta)e^{-\beta H}=A(\tau)$, this equals $\mathrm{Tr}[e^{-\beta H}A(\tau)B]$. Hence $\langle B\,A(\tau-\beta)\rangle=\langle A(\tau)B\rangle=-\mathcal C_{AB}(\tau)$ for $0<\tau<\beta$, and
$$\mathcal C_{AB}(\tau-\beta)=\varepsilon\,\mathcal C_{AB}(\tau).$$
So the sign is $+$ for bosons and $-$ for fermions.

questions.prompt: How is the retarded function $\mathcal C^R_{AB}(\omega)$ obtained from the Matsubara function $\mathcal C_{AB}(i\omega_n)$?
choices: Replace $i\omega_n\to\omega-i\eta$, which gives the advanced function
Take the real part of $\mathcal C_{AB}(i\omega_n)$ and set $\omega_n=\omega$
questions.solution: The Matsubara function is the restriction of an analytic function $\mathcal C_{AB}(z)$ to $z=i\omega_n$. Approaching the real axis from above gives $\mathcal C^R_{AB}$ (Eq. 11.33). The $-i\eta$ continuation gives the advanced function (Eq. 11.34). A naive real-part or Fourier integral is not an analytic continuation.

questions.prompt: Wick's theorem is applied to $\langle T_\tau c_1 c_2 c^\dagger_{2'} c^\dagger_{1'}\rangle_0$ for non-interacting fermions. How many full pairings (terms) appear?
questions.solution: Two annihilation and two creation operators give $2!=2$ pairings: $(1,1')(2,2')$ with sign $+$ and $(1,2')(2,1')$ with sign $-$. This is the determinant of Eq. (11.82). The value 24 counts all orderings of the four operators, which is not the number of pairings.

questions.prompt: Book Exercise 11.2 (redo of Exercise 8.5 in the Matsubara formalism). For a free one-dimensional electron gas with spin, write the current-current Matsubara function in Wick-paired form, evaluate the Matsubara sum with Eq. (11.57), continue $iq_n\to\omega+i\eta$, and take the small-$\omega$ limit of the conductance. Show that the result is $G=2e^2/h$.
questions.solution:
Outline of the worked answer.

1. The current operator of free electrons is $I(q)=\sum_{k\sigma}v_k\,c^\dagger_{k+q\sigma}c_{k\sigma}$ with $v_k=k/m$. The Kubo formula of Sec. 6.3 relates the conductance to the retarded current-current function.
2. Wick's theorem (Eqs. 11.83-11.86) pairs the operators into a single loop, so the Matsubara function is a sum of products $\mathcal G_0(k,\tau)\mathcal G_0(k+q,-\tau)$ weighted by $v_kv_{k+q}$.
3. Fourier transforming and using Eq. (11.57) gives the same structure as Eq. (11.88), with the velocity factors in the numerator.
4. Continue $iq_n\to\omega+i\eta$. Taking $q\to0$ first and then $\omega\to0$ leaves the Fermi-surface term $\propto\sum_{k\sigma}v_k^2\,\delta(\xi_k)$. The two Fermi points and the spin sum give $G=2e^2/h$, the Landauer value for one spin-degenerate channel (Ex. 8.5).

[UNVERIFIED: this is an outline only. The order of limits ($q\to0$ then $\omega\to0$), the spin factor and the $\hbar$ factors were not checked against the full solution of Exercise 8.5.]

questions.prompt: Book Exercise 11.3. Starting from $(-\partial_\tau-\xi)\mathcal G_0(\tau)=\delta(\tau)$ with $\mathcal G_0(\tau)=-\mathcal G_0(\tau+\beta)$, show that $\mathcal G_0(i\omega_n)=1/(i\omega_n-\xi)$ by Fourier transforming the equation.
questions.solution:
Multiply the equation by $e^{i\omega_n\tau}$ and integrate over $(0^+,\beta^-)$. The delta function at $\tau=0$ sits outside this interval, so the right side is zero there. Integrating by parts,
$$-\int_{0^+}^{\beta^-}d\tau\,e^{i\omega_n\tau}\partial_\tau\mathcal G_0=-\Big[e^{i\omega_n\tau}\mathcal G_0\Big]_{0^+}^{\beta^-}+i\omega_n\,\mathcal G_0(i\omega_n).$$
With $e^{i\omega_n\beta}=-1$ and antiperiodicity, $e^{i\omega_n\beta}\mathcal G_0(\beta^-)=\mathcal G_0(0^-)$. The bracket $[e^{i\omega_n\tau}\mathcal G_0]_{0^+}^{\beta^-}$ equals $\mathcal G_0(0^-)-\mathcal G_0(0^+)$. Using $\mathcal G_0(0^-)=n_F$ and $\mathcal G_0(0^+)=-(1-n_F)$, the bracket is 1 and the boundary term $-[\cdots]$ is $-1$. Hence
$$-1+(i\omega_n-\xi)\mathcal G_0(i\omega_n)=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad \mathcal G_0(i\omega_n)=\frac{1}{i\omega_n-\xi}.$$

questions.prompt: Derive the free Matsubara polarizability $\chi_0(q,iq_n)$ from $\chi_0(q,\tau)=-\frac1{\mathcal V}\langle T_\tau\rho(q,\tau)\rho(-q,0)\rangle_0$, with $\rho(q)=\sum_{k\sigma}c^\dagger_{k\sigma}c_{k+q\sigma}$ and $\mathcal G_0(k,i\omega_n)=1/(i\omega_n-\xi_k)$. Show that the Matsubara sum gives the Lindhard form with the $n_F$ difference.
questions.solution:
1. Wick's theorem (Eq. 11.82) keeps only the single-loop pairing. Contracting $c_{k+q}(\tau)$ with $c^\dagger_{k+q}(0)$ and $c^\dagger_k(\tau)$ with $c_k(0)$ gives $\langle T\rho\rho\rangle_0=-\sum_{k\sigma}\mathcal G_0(k+q,\tau)\,\mathcal G_0(k,-\tau)$, so
$$\chi_0(q,\tau)=\frac1{\mathcal V}\sum_{k\sigma}\mathcal G_0(k+q,\tau)\,\mathcal G_0(k,-\tau).$$
2. The Fourier transform of this product is a convolution, so $\chi_0(q,iq_n)=\frac1{\mathcal V}\sum_{k\sigma}\frac1\beta\sum_{ik_n}\mathcal G_0(k,ik_n)\,\mathcal G_0(k+q,ik_n+iq_n)$, with bosonic $iq_n$ and fermionic $ik_n$.
3. The summand is $g(z)=1/[(z-\xi_k)(z+iq_n-\xi_{k+q})]$. Its poles are $z=\xi_k$ and $z=\xi_{k+q}-iq_n$. Eq. (11.57) at $\tau=0$ gives
$$\frac{n_F(\xi_k)}{\xi_k+iq_n-\xi_{k+q}}+\frac{n_F(\xi_{k+q}-iq_n)}{\xi_{k+q}-iq_n-\xi_k}.$$
Because $e^{i\beta q_n}=1$, $n_F(\xi_{k+q}-iq_n)=n_F(\xi_{k+q})$. Hence
$$\chi_0(q,iq_n)=\frac1{\mathcal V}\sum_{k\sigma}\frac{n_F(\xi_k)-n_F(\xi_{k+q})}{iq_n+\xi_k-\xi_{k+q}}.$$
